deck_en: Archimedes could reach exact equality without completing an infinite process—and explained why discovery was not yet proof.
body_en:
# Approaching Without Arriving

## 1. A Book Taken Apart

Early in the thirteenth century, someone needed parchment for a new prayer book. We do not know precisely who made every decision or for which institution the volume was originally intended. We do know what the materials show: older manuscripts were dismantled, their writing partly erased, and their leaves prepared for reuse.

Parchment was expensive. Producing a substantial book required animal skins, labor, and access to suitable materials. An old volume could therefore remain valuable after its contents ceased to be useful to the people holding it. Recycling did not require erasing every trace. It required making the new writing legible enough to serve its purpose.

One of the dismantled books was a tenth-century Greek collection of Archimedes, containing at least seven treatises. Its larger leaves were turned through ninety degrees and folded into the smaller format. Mathematical sentences consequently run across the later prayer-book layout and into folds that concealed them.

Centuries later, those folds would become a conservation problem. Reading the undertext near the spine required taking the book apart again, now that the reused parchment had aged for another seven hundred years. The second disassembly had to undo the consequences of the first without destroying what survived.

A colophon dates the prayer book to April 13, 1229. Its prayers and other evidence point toward Jerusalem or its surroundings. The date is unusually firm; the precise workshop and motives remain less so. Nothing in the evidence requires a campaign against mathematics. Equally, we should not pretend to know the recycler's state of mind. The ordinary economics of parchment provide a sufficient possible explanation without supplying a personal confession.

Archimedes was not the only author reused. The prayer book also incorporates leaves from speeches by an ancient orator, a commentary on Aristotle, and other works. At least seven older books contributed material. From the perspective of the new volume, this was successful manufacture: disparate leaves became a book someone could use.

The old ink did not entirely disappear. Residual material remained in or on the parchment despite washing and scraping. Modern readers could exploit those traces, including the elemental signal from iron-bearing ink. Survival here depended partly on the incompleteness of erasure, not on a continuous decision to preserve the mathematics.

The textual stakes were exceptional. The Method survives through this witness alone. The manuscript also supplies the unique surviving Greek witness to other material, including On Floating Bodies, known through a medieval Latin tradition, and the fragmentary Stomachion, for which related Arabic material also survives. Different kinds of uniqueness should not be collapsed into the claim that everything it contains was otherwise entirely unknown.

The first three essays offered three different relationships between objects and authors: anonymous tablets; named thinkers without autograph objects; a complete transmitted book beside an elusive biography. Here we have both a material object and an author who tells us something specific about his own mathematical work.

But they do not meet in the same century. The parchment collection was copied more than a millennium after Archimedes died. Its stains, folds, glue, and script belong to medieval and later history, not to his desk. Its value comes from the text it transmits and the alternatives it preserves, not from having been touched by the author.

The opening scene is therefore neither a simple tale of destruction nor a miracle of rescue. One use displaced another; material traces survived the change. To recover the mathematical voice, later readers would need to understand both the text and the object that had almost concealed it.

## 2. His Own Voice

Many works of Archimedes begin by addressing a named correspondent. Their greetings frame mathematical treatises, not merely a few private lines. The texts refer to results sent earlier, proofs supplied later, deaths among colleagues, and expectations about what a recipient could accomplish.

Conon, Dositheus, and Eratosthenes belong to this network. The Sand-Reckoner addresses Gelon, associated with the ruling house of Syracuse, and names Archimedes's father as Phidias. These details have a kind of authority absent from much of the earlier material in this series: the transmitted works represent Archimedes speaking rather than a later biographer explaining what he must have been like.

They do not make every modern biographical claim secure. No early evidence establishes the familiar account of his youthful studies in Alexandria. The claim that he was related to Hieron II is clearly attested only much later, in Plutarch. Marriage, children, property, teachers, and domestic habits remain largely inaccessible.

A restrained outline places a mathematician at Syracuse during the reigns of Hieron II and Gelon, in communication with the eastern Mediterranean mathematical world, especially Alexandria, and killed when Syracuse fell to Rome in 212 BCE. That is enough to locate a life without inventing its private rooms.

The preface to On Spirals gives a sharper sense of academic relations. Writing to Dositheus, Archimedes recalls propositions previously sent to Conon and laments that Conon has been dead for years. He expresses confidence in Conon's ability and disappointment that others have not properly dealt with the problems.

Then he acknowledges that two propositions he circulated were deliberately false. Their purpose was to expose people who claimed to have discovered everything but produced no demonstrations. A person claiming success on an impossible proposition could discredit his own boast.

This is not a later character sketch of a prickly genius. It is part of the author's presentation of his mathematical exchange. Results could circulate before proofs. Claims of independent discovery could be asserted. Reputation depended on distinctions between announcing, finding, and demonstrating.

Calling the episode peer review would import a modern institution that did not exist in this form. The more useful comparison concerns the problem, not the name: how can a community evaluate a claim of priority or competence when the claimant need not display the reasoning? False propositions offered Archimedes one means of making an otherwise slippery boast testable.

Physical distance shaped the exchange. In favorable Mediterranean conditions, a voyage across relevant routes might take days or weeks; winds, season, interruptions, and transshipment could extend it considerably. General estimates sometimes give roughly ten days to two weeks for a favorable passage toward Alexandria from Italy, with much slower return travel.

Those are reconstructions of sailing conditions, not measurements of Archimedes's correspondence. No dispatch log survives. Nor do we know the carrier of each mathematical roll. Merchants, official travelers, or trusted intermediaries provide possibilities, not a documented postal system.

The scale nonetheless helps explain the form of the prefaces. A proposition sent ahead of its demonstration could initiate an exchange lasting months. The next communication needed to state what had already been sent, who had since died, what remained unresolved, and why a proof was now being supplied.

Such practical explanations are suggestive rather than exhaustive. Long prefaces also establish authority and shape a reader's response. But they preserve a social texture that finished theorem-proof sequences often hide.

The resulting figure differs from the absent-minded savant of popular anecdote. This Archimedes cares about the order of publication, the abilities of colleagues, the distribution of credit, and the distinction between a claimed result and a demonstrated one. He is not simply lost in mathematics. He is managing how mathematics travels among other people.

## 3. Three Legends

The bath, the final words, and the burning mirrors come from other voices. Their dates and evidential problems differ, so they should not be dismissed—or believed—as one package.

Vitruvius, writing in the first century BCE, gives the familiar crown story almost two centuries after Archimedes's death. Hieron suspects that a goldsmith has substituted silver in a votive crown. Archimedes must investigate without destroying it. Water displaced as he enters a bath supplies the insight, followed by an ecstatic run and the famous cry of discovery.

Vitruvius describes comparing the water displaced by equal weights of gold, silver, and the crown. The physical principle is sound: equal masses of materials with different densities occupy different volumes. The difficulty is the particular measuring procedure, especially if only a small fraction of the gold has been replaced.

Galileo argued in his 1586 discussion of the little balance that collecting overflow would be too crude for the required discrimination. Wetting, adhesion, surface effects, splashing, and uncertainty over exactly filling a vessel can rival the volume difference being measured. Later analyses developed these objections.

It is too strong to say that the operation is physically impossible in every conceivable setup. Its success depends on object size, adulteration, apparatus, and precision. The historically responsible criticism is that the familiar account does not establish a sufficiently controlled assay. A correct principle does not authenticate the episode or its procedure.

Hydrostatic weighing offers a more precise alternative by comparing apparent weight in air and water. Galileo explained such a method. Its feasibility does not show that Archimedes actually used it for a crown. Modern reconstruction answers what could work, not what happened.

The death narratives have a different problem: incompatible motives and expanding dialogue. Livy gives a relatively spare account of Archimedes intent on figures when an unrecognizing soldier kills him during the sack. Marcellus regrets the death and honors the family. Valerius Maximus later gives the mathematician a plea that his work not be disturbed.

Plutarch, around the beginning of the second century CE, openly preserves alternatives. In one, Archimedes refuses to leave an unfinished demonstration when ordered to meet Marcellus, provoking the soldier. In another, he asks an approaching killer to wait until the problem is complete. In a third, soldiers mistake mathematical instruments he is carrying for valuables and kill him for plunder.

The celebrated wording about not disturbing his circles is not a securely recorded verbatim last utterance. The surviving variants support a tradition about mathematical absorption amid violence, not a transcript. Nor does their chronological order prove that each author embellished the immediately preceding author. Lost common sources and parallel traditions remain possible.

The mirrors require a third test. Polybius, much nearer the siege, describes defensive machines, projectiles at different ranges, and attacks on ships. Livy gives gripping details of openings in the walls, missiles, and grappling devices capable of lifting and dropping a vessel's bow. Plutarch also emphasizes machinery. These accounts do not describe the familiar array of burning mirrors.

Later references to ships destroyed by fire appear before the detailed mirror tradition. Lucian alludes to burning; Anthemius of Tralles, around the sixth century, belongs to the much later history of explicitly reconstructing burning mirrors. Distance from the siege grows as the optical apparatus becomes more elaborate.

Modern demonstrations show that concentrated sunlight can char or ignite a stationary wooden target. A widely discussed 2005 experiment used 127 roughly one-foot-square mirrors at about thirty meters. Favorable weather and sustained alignment mattered. Accounts of such trials do not establish a practical siege weapon: moving ships, imperfect aim, orientation, range, and clouds radically complicate the task.

The distinction is between optical possibility and military utility. Conventional incendiaries could deliver fire with fewer simultaneous conditions. Neither a successful demonstration nor a failed television experiment by itself decides the ancient history.

All three legends place Archimedes against an external force: a suspicious king, a soldier's weapon, an enemy fleet. His own surviving prefaces instead discuss correspondence, colleagues, and demonstrations. Plutarch explains the missing engineering treatises by portraying Archimedes as disdainful of useful mechanical arts, then links that attitude to stories about Plato's disapproval of mechanical geometry.

That portrait deserves comparison with the author's own Method, where an imagined balance is central to discovery. It does not prove that every report of his philosophical preferences is false. It does prevent a later moralized opposition between pure geometry and mechanics from speaking uncontested on his behalf.

## 4. Two Contradictions, One Exact Result

The so-called method of exhaustion is often described as adding sides until a polygon becomes infinitely sided and therefore becomes a circle. That image is suggestive, but it misses the logical structure of the classical demonstrations.

Begin with a definite candidate for a curvilinear area, perhaps the area of a specified rectilinear figure. Suppose the actual area is larger. Then there is a particular positive difference between the two. Construct a finite inscribed approximation fine enough that its uncovered remainder is smaller than that difference. Using established geometrical relations, derive incompatible inequalities.

Next suppose the actual area is smaller than the candidate. An appropriate complementary construction yields another contradiction. The precise arrangement varies with the theorem; not every proof has an identical pair of inscribed and circumscribed figures. The essential structure excludes both possible inequalities and leaves equality.

At no point must the polygon acquire an actually infinite number of sides. Every contradiction is reached at a finite stage selected in response to a specified positive discrepancy. The universal strength comes from the guarantee that no proposed positive gap can survive the procedure.

This is the distinction between an image of an endless process and a proof of control. The picture suggests closer and closer approach. The argument establishes that any alleged difference can be defeated by some finite construction. Exactness does not wait for a final infinite operation.

Euclid X.1 provides a standard tool: if more than half of a magnitude is repeatedly removed, the remainder eventually becomes smaller than a prescribed smaller magnitude. Its background includes an Archimedean relation among magnitudes. The point is not to complete infinitely many subtractions; it is to establish a finite stage below any given threshold.

Its position at the beginning of Book X makes it reusable. A proposition about reducing magnitudes can support proofs about many different figures. The later label “exhaustion” collects related techniques that ancient authors did not necessarily present under one unified methodological title.

In Measurement of a Circle, Archimedes proves that a circle has the area of a right triangle whose perpendicular sides equal the radius and circumference. He also bounds the circumference-to-diameter ratio between 3 + 10/71 and 3 + 1/7. Controlled polygonal constructions and square-root estimates produce inequalities, not a decimal asserted to be the circumference itself.

Quadrature of the Parabola establishes that a parabolic segment has four-thirds the area of a particular inscribed triangle. The work offers more than one route, including a mechanical argument involving equilibrium and a geometrical treatment. Its preface already distinguishes discovery by mechanical means from the subsequent organization of a demonstration.

On the Sphere and Cylinder moves the control into three dimensions. The surface area of a sphere is four times the area of its great circle. Its volume is two-thirds that of the circumscribed cylinder of equal radius and height equal to the sphere's diameter. The demonstrations do not simply declare a sphere to be the sum of infinitely thin discs and stop. Finite geometrical comparisons carry the deductive burden.

The standard historical label is commonly traced to Gregory of Saint-Vincent's seventeenth-century work, especially his 1647 treatment of quadratures. The terminology can create the misleading impression of one named invention passed intact from one founder to successors. The ancient materials instead display interrelated practices: proportion, indirect proof, finite approximation, and arbitrarily small remainders.

Archimedes himself gives unusually valuable evidence about credit. In the Method he says that Eudoxus first demonstrated the one-third relation between a cone and the corresponding cylinder, and between a pyramid and the corresponding prism. He also credits Democritus with earlier statements of the results without proof.

This testimony does not supply every detail of their methods. It does show an author distinguishing at least three achievements: stating a result, proving it, and providing a way to discover it. Mathematical credit can be divided because these accomplishments are not identical. The next section concerns the third—and a text whose survival nearly failed.

## 5. The Method

The work addresses Eratosthenes with a greeting. Archimedes recalls propositions previously sent without demonstrations and now supplies further material. He also explains a mechanical procedure for discovering mathematical relations. Its central instrument is a balance imagined within the reasoning.

Consider a plane figure through parallel line segments, or a solid through parallel sections. Compare corresponding segments or sections, establish relations among their lengths or areas, and imagine arranging the associated weights on a lever. Appropriate distances from the fulcrum make each corresponding pair balance.

The reasoning then passes from the slices to the figures they represent. If all the corresponding parts satisfy the required balance relation, the whole figures appear to bear a determinate relation of weight and therefore of area or volume. Known centers of gravity help turn that equilibrium into the desired result.

The procedure is powerful because it supplies a target. Instead of searching blindly for an exact area, the geometer has a reason to expect one particular relation. But Archimedes expressly distinguishes such discovery from the final demonstration he considers necessary.

This is not merely a later historian deciding that ancient reasoning falls short of modern rigor. The distinction occurs in the author's own methodological statement. Mechanical investigation can reveal a theorem; geometrical proof must then establish it in the required sense.

He explains the practical benefit without mystification. Knowing what conclusion to seek makes finding a proof easier than working without a target. His discussion of Democritus and Eudoxus reinforces the difference between having the right result and possessing its demonstration.

He also explains why he is communicating the procedure. Other mathematicians, including future readers, might use it to discover results he has not found. The text presents method as something transferable, not merely as a retrospective decoration around the author's genius.

Calling this “secret calculus” misses the point. Archimedes is not confessing that he covertly used a forbidden modern theory. He is openly distinguishing two jobs. One procedure generates credible conjectures and directs inquiry. Another secures conclusions by the standards of demonstrative geometry.

That distinction sounds ordinary to readers trained to separate intuition from proof. Its explicit, first-person form is nevertheless unusual among surviving advanced Greek mathematical texts. Most show propositions arranged after the exploratory work is complete. The reader receives a finished road rather than a record of how its builder searched for a route.

The Method lets us hear something closer to “this is how I found it.” Even so, it is not an unedited laboratory notebook. Archimedes has selected examples and crafted an exposition. We should not assume that every false start or actual chronological step appears.

Nor is it the only ancient discussion of discovery. The Quadrature already refers to mechanical and geometrical approaches. Pappus later discusses analysis and synthesis: reasoning from what is sought and then reversing the route into a demonstration. Such comparisons prevent a rhetorical claim of absolute uniqueness from outrunning the archive.

The special value lies in the combination: a major mathematician explicitly differentiates heuristic and demonstrative procedures and explains in detail how they cooperate. The mechanical procedure is not worthless because it is not the final proof. Its value consists partly in reducing the field of possibilities.

The resemblance to seventeenth-century methods of indivisibles is undeniable. Both involve comparing figures through slices or associated collections of lower-dimensional elements. Familiarity can, however, create a false route of transmission.

The Method was not available to the European mathematicians developing those seventeenth-century techniques. It reentered scholarship only after its identification in 1906. Other Archimedean works deeply influenced early modern mathematics; this particular text cannot be treated as a document they read.

The defensible relation is structural comparison, not demonstrated instruction across the centuries. Similar problems can encourage similar techniques without a surviving channel from one formulation to the other. Recovering the Method enlarged our knowledge of ancient reasoning. It did not retroactively put the rediscovered book on Cavalieri's desk.

## 6. Infinity Without a Decree

In Book III of the Physics, Aristotle distinguishes an infinity that is always available for further continuation from an infinite magnitude already complete. No matter how far one has proceeded, more can be taken or further division made. He argues that mathematicians need not possess a completed infinite quantity in order to work.

That philosophical position fits much of the classical geometrical practice just described. A proof can choose an arbitrarily large but finite construction or reduce a remainder below an arbitrarily prescribed positive magnitude. It does not need a last stage after infinitely many operations.

Compatibility is not a documented command. The tidy causal chain—Zeno creates a difficulty, Aristotle bans actual infinity, mathematicians obey, and exhaustion is invented—does not follow from the sources. Eudoxus belongs to the same century as Aristotle and precedes much of his philosophical writing. His techniques cannot simply be explained as compliance with a later published rule.

No Archimedean preface says that a proof has been designed to satisfy Aristotle's prohibition. It is equally possible that philosophical accounts partly described and interpreted existing mathematical practice. Influence may have worked through a shared intellectual setting rather than through a decree issued to a professional community.

The palimpsest complicates even the generalization that Greek mathematicians never entertained completed infinite collections. Reviel Netz's readings of parts of the Method emphasize passages apparently treating all the relevant lines or sections together, sometimes in language concerning their multiplicity or number.

On that interpretation, Archimedes's heuristic reasoning admits an operational totality of infinitely many elements. Other scholars caution that translating such language into a completed infinite set can import modern set-theoretic commitments not present in the text. A geometrical totality of sections is not automatically a theory of infinite cardinality.

The author's own distinction between mechanical discovery and formal proof also matters. A mode of reasoning used to locate a result need not be an accepted foundation for its demonstration. The same mathematician can permit an exploratory picture and require a different argument before treating the theorem as established.

This is a genuine interpretive dispute, not a choice between mathematical enlightenment and ancient timidity. Scholars are debating the force of particular words and procedures. Some of those words became more legible only through modern recovery of a physically damaged manuscript.

Two blanket claims should therefore be avoided. Greek thought was not governed by an exceptionless rule preventing every actual-infinite idea from entering mathematical inquiry. But Archimedes did not thereby possess modern infinite-set theory. A more defensible formulation describes a preference in formal geometrical demonstration, with a less uniform range of heuristic practices.

The Sand-Reckoner addresses another confusion: the difference between unimaginably large and infinite. Some people, Archimedes says, believe that sand cannot be counted or that no available number could name its quantity. He extends the naming system for numbers and sets generous assumptions about the size of the cosmos.

The task is not to count the actual grains in the universe. It is to show that even filling an enormously enlarged universe with sand would yield a finite quantity within the reach of a constructed numerical vocabulary. The failure of familiar names is not proof of infinity.

The work also preserves an important account of Aristarchus of Samos. Archimedes describes hypotheses in which the Sun and fixed stars remain at rest while the Earth travels around the Sun, with the stellar sphere placed at an immense distance. Aristarchus's own heliocentric treatise is lost.

This is one of the earliest and most explicit surviving technical reports of that proposal, not its only ancient trace. Plutarch and later doxographical traditions also refer to an Earth in motion. The distinction repeats the larger lesson: a uniquely valuable witness need not be the sole witness to everything it mentions.

Archimedes's own words thus complicate the simplified image in several directions. He disciplines approximation without completing an infinite process, explores mechanical totalities whose interpretation remains contested, and constructs numbers large enough to defeat a claim of uncountability. Those are related concerns, not one uniform attitude captured by the word infinity.

## 7. The Tomb Cicero Says He Found

A more substantial piece of personal evidence comes from Cicero. Plutarch reports that Archimedes wanted the sphere and cylinder placed on his tomb because he prized the result about them. That statement is late. Cicero supplies a different kind of claim: an account of something he says he did himself.

Writing the Tusculan Disputations around 45 BCE, Cicero recalls his service as quaestor in Sicily in 75 BCE. He says the Syracusans no longer knew the location of Archimedes's tomb. Remembering verses and the identifying sphere-and-cylinder device, he searched near the Agrigentine gate and noticed a small column rising through undergrowth.

He had the vegetation cleared and examined a partially damaged inscription. The event he narrates occurred about 137 years after Archimedes's death, but the gap between Cicero's claimed visit and his written recollection was only about thirty years. Those are two different chronological distances.

This is stronger than a report that someone had heard of a bathroom revelation two centuries earlier. Cicero claims personal contact with a site, a marker, vegetation, and an inscription. Yet a first-person claim is not immune to scrutiny. We cannot follow a continuous identity chain from the monument he describes to a securely identified object today.

He might have accepted a local attribution or mistaken a monument. His account is also self-presentational. The cultivated outsider from Arpinum restores to a famous Greek city knowledge of its own greatest intellectual citizen. The local forgetfulness makes the Roman discoverer's learning shine.

The context supplies another reason not to read the passage as a neutral excavation report. Cicero is discussing whether virtue can suffice for happiness. He contrasts the life of the mathematician with that of the Syracusan tyrant Dionysius. Inquiry nourishes one mind; violence and fear poison the other.

The tomb episode gives material form to that moral comparison. The modest figure absorbed in diagrams becomes preferable to the powerful ruler. This literary purpose does not make the visit fictitious, but it helps explain why it is narrated and which features receive emphasis.

The strongest defensible statement is precise: Cicero says that in 75 BCE he found and cleared a tomb which he identified from a sphere-and-cylinder marker and inscription as Archimedes's. The further claim that Archimedes personally ordered that monument design comes from a later source. The two should not be fused into one eyewitness testimony.

The mathematical emblem itself is well chosen. The sphere-and-cylinder relation genuinely belongs to the transmitted Archimedean achievement. That congruence strengthens the identification's intelligibility without removing its historical limits.

Chronology again reveals unequal certainty. The death in 212 BCE is attached to the sack of Syracuse during the Second Punic War and to several accounts placing Archimedes in that setting. The customary birth date around 287 BCE has a much weaker basis.

It is derived from the twelfth-century writer John Tzetzes's statement that Archimedes lived seventy-five years. Subtracting that age from the accepted death year produces a date that later timelines display with deceptively equal confidence. The arithmetic is straightforward; the authority of the age report is not.

This is how a precise-looking year can lose its provenance. A late statement of age becomes an inferred birth year, then a printed range, then an apparently solid biographical fact. Precision of calculation has concealed uncertainty of input.

Absolute dates for individual treatises are also mostly reconstructions. Prefaces give relative order: a result had already been circulated; Conon had died; Dositheus received a subsequent communication; the Method looks back on earlier mechanical findings. That is genuine chronological information, but it does not place a calendar date beneath every work.

The prayer book's colophon is, in this respect, more definite than much of the mathematician's life. April 13, 1229 is physically written into a later object. A confident date may tell us exactly when Archimedes was overwritten while his own sequence of composition remains only partly recoverable.

## 8. More Than a Millennium

The modern recovery did not begin with a chance visit in 1906. Constantin von Tischendorf saw the palimpsest in Constantinople in the 1840s and noticed mathematical undertext. A leaf from the volume later reached Cambridge University Library through his estate.

In 1899, Athanasios Papadopoulos-Kerameus catalogued the manuscript as number 355 in a collection associated with the Jerusalem patriarchate's Constantinople dependency. He transcribed a few visible lines. Johan Ludvig Heiberg recognized material from On the Sphere and Cylinder and traveled to examine the book in 1906.

Heiberg worked with eyesight, magnification, lighting, and contemporary photography, not modern multispectral equipment. He identified seven Archimedean works, most sensationally the Method. Another visit followed in 1908. A catalogue entry and a trained reader's recognition had opened a text absent from the familiar printed tradition.

The photographic record is easy to miscount. Accounts distinguish individual exposures from photographed pages or openings: roughly sixty-five photographs can cover more than a hundred written sides because some show a double opening. Those images later became witnesses in their own right.

The book deteriorated after Heiberg saw it. Mold destroyed some material; leaves disappeared; later interventions obscured others. A photograph could preserve a reading no longer recoverable from the object. “Consult the original” does not always mean “consult the richest surviving evidence.”

The ownership history between its early twentieth-century examination and its appearance in French private hands is incomplete and contested. At the 1998 sale, the Greek Orthodox side argued that it had left church custody unlawfully; a French family asserted an earlier private acquisition. A real manuscript does not automatically carry a complete provenance.

An anonymous private buyer acquired it at auction in New York for about two million dollars and supported a long program of conservation, imaging, and scholarship at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore. The public project documentation does not authorize attaching an unverified famous person's name to that owner.

Conservation came before spectacular imaging. The book could not safely be treated as a stack of pages ready for scanning. Modern adhesive in the spine was tenacious, while mold-damaged parchment could be friable. Disbinding proceeded over years, from 2000 to 2004, with the risk that solving one problem might aggravate another.

Multispectral imaging separated information by taking images under different wavelengths and combining their responses. Parchment, the prayer text, and the underlying mathematical ink do not respond identically across ultraviolet, visible, and infrared illumination. Later campaigns used twelve spectral bands and raking light. This was not simply a sharper photograph but an analysis of different physical signals.

Forged images of evangelists added in the twentieth century presented another obstacle. Their models can be traced to a publication of 1929, establishing a lower limit for their manufacture. Paint and gold could block the optical view of writing beneath them.

X-ray fluorescence offered another route. Intense X-rays excite elements in the ink; characteristic emissions can be mapped point by point. Iron distributions helped recover letter forms even under overlying material. Work at the Stanford synchrotron made this technique part of the palimpsest's recovery.

The resulting images did not restore everything. No imaging method can extract writing from parchment and ink that have physically vanished, or read a leaf that is absent from the object being scanned. Statements that technology has recovered the entire book confuse enhancement of surviving signals with reversal of material loss.

The inventory itself continues to change. In October 2025, a missing leaf was identified in the Museum of Fine Arts in Blois by comparison with Heiberg's photographs. It contains material from On the Sphere and Cylinder. The rediscovery was announced in 2026; the recent institutional report confirms that the manuscript's history is still being revised, not merely retold.

The main prayer-book volume is described as containing about 174 parchment leaves—roughly 348 written sides—with leaves around twenty by fifteen centimeters. Counting leaves, pages, and exposures as though they were interchangeable would distort the physical object.

Within the transmission of Archimedes, the tenth-century copy is exceptionally early and sometimes uniquely informative. It is not physically close to his lifetime. Depending on where within that century the copying is placed, well over eleven centuries separate it from 212 BCE; the frequently used figure of about 1,180 years is an approximation, not an exact dated interval.

Its parchment and medieval minuscule are not things Archimedes knew. Much older physical witnesses to Greek mathematics survive, including Roman-period fragments of Euclid. What makes this object extraordinary is the combination of age within its particular tradition, unique textual contents, and recoverable material evidence.

The Method reached us through skins, ink, folding, libraries, cataloguing, travel, photography, conservation, spectral analysis, and X-rays. Chance operated at more than one point; conscious labor operated at many. It would be another neat legend to assign accident exclusively to the medieval scraper and perfect foresight to everyone afterward.

At the beginning stands an act of reuse that nearly removed a text. At the end stands an author's explanation that discovery and proof do different work. The exact equality did not require a polygon finally to become a circle. The survival of that explanation, however, required very particular things to remain: marks, fibers, pages, and readers capable of recognizing what they were seeing.
